terms.grammar: pronoun, second person: dative tibi, accusative and ablative tē; plural vōs
evidence: Plaut. Curc. 516–516d: Heus tū, tibi ego dīcō.
Ter. Ph. 556: ūnā tēcum bona mala tolerābimus
terms.comment: As with ego, the verb’s ending says “you”, and tū is added only for stress or contrast: Quō nunc abīs? quīn tū hīc manēs? Latin says tū to anyone, a parent, a master or a stranger; there is no polite plural. “With you” is tēcum. Stronger, tūte (comedy) and tūte ipse.

phrases.latin: Quō nunc abīs? quīn tū hīc manēs?
phrases.english: Where are you off to now? Why don’t you stay here?

phrases.latin: numquid vīs? — Bene valē. — Valē. — Heus tū, tibi ego dīcō.
phrases.english: Anything else? — Goodbye. — Goodbye. — Hey, you! I’m talking to you.

phrases.latin: Salvum tē advenīre, Dēmea, gaudēmus. — Ehem, opportūnē: tē ipsum quaeritō.
phrases.english: We’re glad to see you safely here, Demea. — Ah, just in time: you’re the very man I’m looking for.

phrases.latin: Nōlī metuere: ūnā tēcum bona mala tolerābimus.
phrases.english: Don’t be afraid: we’ll bear good and bad together with you.

phrases.latin: difficilis facilis, jūcundus acerbus es īdem: nec tēcum possum vīvere, nec sine tē
phrases.english: Hard and easy, sweet and sour, you are both at once: I can’t live with you, or without you.

phrases.latin: Tūte hoc intrīstī: tibi omne est exedendum.
phrases.english: You cooked this up yourself: you must eat it all up.

sources: Lewis & Short: tu · Lewis & Short: tute
